extra_info: ENSO stands for El Niño–Southern Oscillation, a natural climate pattern involving changes in tropical Pacific Ocean temperatures and the atmosphere. El Niño is the pattern's warm phase and can influence weather in many parts of the world.
task_instruction: Answer each negative question with a short answer that matches the facts.
paragraphs: A fictional climate research team is preparing a public briefing about El Niño and long-term global warming. Researcher Nia reviews a graph and asks, {{red:Isn't El Niño a natural climate pattern?}} The team's reference guide describes it as a naturally occurring pattern, so colleague Omar answers, {{mask_1}}. Nia points to a separate line on the graph and asks, {{red:Doesn't the graph show a long-term rise in global average temperature?}} The line rises across several decades, so Omar replies, {{mask_2}}. Nia checks the meeting notes and asks, {{red:Haven't the researchers separated short-term variation from the long-term trend?}} The team has made two separate sections in the briefing, so Omar says, {{mask_3}}. A draft caption is still missing. Nia asks, {{red:Hasn't someone written a caption for this chart?}} The caption field is blank, so Omar answers, {{mask_4}}.

The team reviews a map of ocean temperatures. Nia asks, {{red:Isn't the warm-water area shown in the central and eastern tropical Pacific?}} The map labels that region, so Omar replies, {{mask_5}}. Another map shows rainfall patterns. Nia asks, {{red:Doesn't the map show rainfall changing in every region in the same way?}} The colors differ by region, so Omar answers, {{mask_6}}. Omar opens the data notes and asks, {{red:Haven't the notes listed the source of each dataset?}} Every dataset has a source citation, so Nia says, {{mask_7}}. A student asks about a forecast. Nia replies with a question, {{red:Can one seasonal forecast describe exactly what the weather will be every day?}} The team explains that it cannot, so Omar answers, {{mask_8}}.

During the briefing, Nia discusses the difference between climate and weather. She asks, {{red:Isn't weather the condition of the atmosphere over a short period?}} The team's glossary gives that definition, so Omar says, {{mask_9}}. Nia asks, {{red:Doesn't climate describe patterns over longer periods?}} The glossary says it does, so Omar replies, {{mask_10}}. A slide mentions greenhouse gases. Nia asks, {{red:Haven't human activities increased the amount of some greenhouse gases in the atmosphere?}} The cited report documents an increase, so Omar answers, {{mask_11}}. Then she points to a note about El Niño and asks, {{red:Isn't every El Niño event exactly the same?}} The research notes describe differences between events, so Omar says, {{mask_12}}.

Before the audience arrives, the team checks its slides. Nia asks, {{red:Hasn't the team checked the figures against the source tables?}} Two researchers have checked them, so Omar replies, {{mask_13}}. Nia looks at a chart title and asks, {{red:Isn't this chart showing a single year's data?}} It combines data from many years, so Omar answers, {{mask_14}}. Omar checks the printed handouts and asks, {{red:Have we included a note explaining the limits of the forecast?}} The note is on the final page, so Nia says, {{mask_15}}. The room is still empty. Nia asks, {{red:Aren't the audience members here yet?}} The doors have not opened, so Omar replies, {{mask_16}}.

The briefing begins, and the team presents its evidence carefully. After the talk, an audience member asks whether El Niño alone explains long-term warming. Nia responds, {{red:Doesn't the briefing say that one climate pattern alone explains the whole long-term warming trend?}} The briefing says it does not, so Omar answers, {{mask_17}}. Another person asks about local effects. Nia asks, {{red:Can the same local impact be assumed for every El Niño event?}} The team has explained that effects vary, so Omar replies, {{mask_18}}. After the questions, Nia reviews the feedback cards and asks, {{red:Haven't some audience members requested more information about the data?}} Several cards ask for the data sources, so Omar says, {{mask_19}}. The team plans to publish its references online. Nia asks, {{red:Shouldn't the references be available with the briefing?}} The editor has approved a page containing all the references, so Omar answers, {{mask_20}}.
